concepts.summary: Wherever people live beside water, they give it inhabitants. Springs, rivers, lakes and seas acquire resident persons (nymphs, lords, brides, lurkers) who grant fish and fertility or drag the careless under. The pattern is so widespread that no single origin is needed: water gives life and takes it without warning, and a personal spirit makes both habits intelligible and open to negotiation by gift, courtesy or cunning. Some regional families do share descent or borrowing, as the water-women of Slavic, Finnic and Germanic folklore trade traits across borders, but most resemblances here are independent answers to the same wet and dangerous facts.

versions.title: The Daughters of Nereus
versions.teaser: Fifty sea-daughters named like weather, and a spring nymph who kept Hylas.
versions.text:
Hesiod lists them by name: the fifty daughters of Nereus, the truthful Old Man of the Sea, and Doris, child of Ocean. Among them are Galene ‘Calm’, Kymo ‘Wave’, Glauke ‘Sea-grey’, Thetis and Amphitrite, and the catalogue reads like a sailor's vocabulary of the weather. Fresh water has its own nymphs: Ocean and Tethys, Hesiod says, have three thousand daughters and as many river sons, and every spring and stream has its Naiad.

These are not remote goddesses. The Nereids rise from the sea with Thetis to mourn Patroclus, and they ride in Poseidon's train. River and spring nymphs are more dangerous. In the Argonautica young Hylas goes to draw water at the spring of Pegae; its nymph, dazzled by his beauty in the moonlight, puts her arm around his neck and draws him down into the pool. Heracles searches the shore shouting his name, and the Argo sails without either of them.

image.caption: Thetis and the Nereids bring Achilles his new armour; Attic red-figure krater, c. 460 BCE, Louvre

versions.title: A Bride for the River Earl
versions.teaser: Each year the shamans drowned a bride; one magistrate sent the shamans instead.
versions.text:
Hebo, the Earl of the Yellow River, is a vain spirit. In the Zhuangzi he swells with pride at the autumn floods, then reaches the sea, meets Ruo of the North Sea, and understands for the first time how small he is.

He is also hungry. The Shiji tells how in Ye, in the state of Wei, the shamans and local elders chose a girl every year as the River Earl's bride, dressed her, set her on a bridal couch and floated it out until it sank, collecting a heavy tax for the ceremony. The new magistrate, Ximen Bao, attended the next wedding. He inspected the girl, declared her not beautiful enough, and asked the old chief shamaness to go and tell the Earl a better bride would come later. His soldiers threw her into the river. When she did not return, he sent her disciples after her, then an elder. The rest knocked their heads on the ground until they bled, and the weddings stopped. Ximen Bao then dug twelve canals.
sources: Sima Qian, Shiji 126 (supplement by Chu Shaosun)

versions.title: Rán's Net
versions.teaser: The sea-giant's wife nets the drowned; her nine daughters are the waves.
versions.text:
Rán is the wife of the sea-giant Ægir, and she owns a net in which she catches those who drown. Their nine daughters are the waves, and Snorri gives their names: Himinglæva ‘Heaven-bright’, Blóðughadda ‘Bloody-hair’, Hrönn, Bylgja, Dúfa, Kólga and the rest.

The net has other uses. In the prose of Reginsmál, Loki borrows it to catch the dwarf Andvari, who lives as a pike beneath a waterfall and must give up his gold. But mostly Rán's catch is human. When the poet Egill Skallagrímsson loses his son Böðvarr at sea, he complains in Sonatorrek that Rán has torn a gap in his kin, and says that if a sword could settle the matter he would fight Ægir. Eyrbyggja saga preserves a gentler belief: drowned men who appeared at their own funeral feast were thought to have been well received by Rán.

image.caption: The Daughters of Rán, by Hans Dahl

versions.title: She of the Jade Skirt
versions.teaser: The goddess of lakes and streams overturns canoes and washes the newborn.
versions.text:
Chalchiuhtlicue, ‘She of the Jade Skirt’, is the goddess of the waters on the ground: springs, rivers, lagoons and the lake around Tenochtitlan. Sahagún's informants call her the elder sister of the rain gods, the Tlaloque. She has power over the waters of sea and river: she can raise storms and whirlpools, overturn canoes and drown those who travel on the water. Those who live by water, the water-sellers and the canoe-men, honour her with festivals.

She is also the first water a person touches. When a child is born, the midwife bathes it and addresses the goddess, asking her to wash away whatever harm the child has brought with it into the world. In the Codex Borbonicus she sits enthroned while a great stream flows from beneath her, carrying away a man and a woman, a clear picture of how her gifts and dangers come together.

image.caption: Chalchiuhtlicue enthroned above her stream, detail of the Codex Borbonicus, 16th century

versions.title: The Kappa's Dish
versions.teaser: A river imp with a water-filled head can be undone by a polite bow.
versions.text:
The kappa, ‘river child’, is the best-known water spirit of Japanese folklore: a child-sized creature with a beak, a shell, webbed hands and a hollow dish on top of its head that holds water. It lurks in rivers and ponds, drags horses and children into the water, and is said to pull out a victim's shirikodama, a mythical ball inside the body. It is fond of cucumbers.

Its strength depends on the water in its dish. Since the kappa is scrupulously polite, the traveller who bows to it will be bowed to in return, and the water spills out, leaving the creature helpless. Many local tales describe a captured kappa bargaining for release, promising never again to harm the village or teaching its captor the secret of setting broken bones. Edo-period scholars catalogued it under names such as kawatarō, and illustrators drew it again and again.
versions.caveat: The kappa is a folk creature with many regional names and forms, recorded mainly from the Edo period onward, not a figure of the ancient chronicles.

image.caption: A kappa, by Toriyama Sekien, 18th century

versions.title: Taniwha of the Deep Pools
versions.teaser: Guardians of rivers and harbours, and sometimes man-eaters in dark caves.
versions.text:
Taniwha live in deep river pools, dark caves, harbour mouths and dangerous currents. They take many shapes, from shark or giant lizard to a floating log, and they are ambiguous. Many are kaitiaki, guardians who protect a particular people and warn them of danger; a well-known saying calls the Waikato River ‘Waikato taniwha rau’, Waikato of a hundred taniwha, with a taniwha at every bend, a figure that also honours the river's many chiefs.

Others are killers. Among the stories George Grey published is that of Hotupuku, a monster of the Rotorua district who devoured travellers on the road. The warriors lure it from its lair, catch it in strong ropes and kill it, and when they cut it open they find inside the bodies of men, women and children along with their weapons and garments. The same waters could guard a people or eat them, depending on who the taniwha was and whom it served.

versions.title: The Lady of Llyn y Fan Fach
versions.teaser: A lake-woman marries a farmer and warns him: three causeless blows.
versions.text:
A young farmer of Blaensawdde, near Myddfai, sees a beautiful woman sitting on the surface of the lake Llyn y Fan Fach. He offers her bread. The first loaf, hard-baked, she refuses; the second, unbaked, she refuses; the third, lightly baked, she accepts. She agrees to marry him on one condition: if he strikes her three causeless blows, she will return to the lake.

Her father rises from the water with two identical daughters, and the farmer must pick his bride; he knows her by how she ties her sandal. Her dowry of cattle, sheep and horses comes up out of the lake. Years pass. He taps her with a glove when she is slow to go to a christening, again when she weeps at a wedding, and a third time when she laughs at a funeral. She walks back into the lake, calling her cattle after her; the ploughing oxen follow, dragging the plough behind them. Later she appears to her son Rhiwallon and teaches him the medicine of the Physicians of Myddfai.
sources: The Physicians of Myddvai (1861), introductory legend
versions.caveat: The legend was first printed in the nineteenth century, though the Physicians of Myddfai themselves appear in medieval Welsh medical manuscripts.

versions.title: Rusalki in the Birches
versions.teaser: Drowned girls leave the river at Rusalia week to swing and tickle.
versions.text:
In Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian village belief the rusalki are the restless dead: most often girls who drowned or died before marriage, sometimes unbaptized children. They live in rivers and lakes for most of the year, but in the week around Trinity, Rusalia week, they come out. They sit in the birches and swing on the branches, comb their long loose hair, dance in the rye fields, and call to passing young men, whom they may tickle or dance to death.

Villagers kept careful rules that week: women hung cloth and thread on the trees as gifts, people avoided bathing, and some carried wormwood as protection. At the end of the week many villages performed a ‘seeing-off of the rusalka’, escorting a straw figure or a costumed girl out to the fields or the river. Southern accounts make the rusalki pale and beautiful, with green hair; northern ones make them frightening.
sources: Dmitry Zelenin, Essays on Russian Mythology (1916)
versions.caveat: This is village belief recorded by 19th- and 20th-century ethnographers, with much regional variation; the romantic mermaid-rusalka of later literature is a further development.

image.caption: Mermaids (Rusalki), by Ivan Kramskoi, 1871

versions.title: The Great Lynx of the Lake
versions.teaser: A horned, spiny water-panther guards the copper and raises storms.
versions.text:
Beneath the waters of Lake Superior and the other Great Lakes lives Mishipeshu, the Great Lynx or underwater panther: a long-tailed cat with horns and a spined back, sometimes described with a tail of copper. It stirs up storms, whirlpools and sudden rapids, and drowns those who cross its waters without respect. The native copper of the lake country belongs to it, and taking it is risky.

Mishipeshu is the great enemy of the Thunderbirds, who fight it from the sky; the lightning striking the water is part of that war. Before a dangerous crossing, travellers offered tobacco to the waters to secure a safe passage. On Agawa Rock, on the shore of Lake Superior, a red ochre painting shows the horned, spiny creature beside canoes and serpents: one of the best-known images of the water-lord, painted where the lake is at its most dangerous.
sources: Selwyn Dewdney and Kenneth Kidd, Indian Rock Paintings of the Great Lakes (1962)

image.caption: The underwater panther Mishipeshu, pictograph on Agawa Rock, Lake Superior

concepts.summary: A rich city, a moment of pride or carelessness, and then the water closes over the rooftops. Tales of drowned cities cluster along coasts and lakeshores from Wales and Brittany to Russia, India and China, often with the detail that bells can still be heard beneath the waves. Real losses surely feed them: coastlines do sink, earthquakes do drown towns, as Greek Helike was drowned in 373 BCE. But the stories are also moral devices, turning geography into judgment. Their resemblances are best explained by common experience and by shared Christian and hagiographic motifs within Europe, not by one ancient source.

versions.title: Atlantis
versions.teaser: A proud island empire beyond the Pillars sinks in one day and night.
versions.text:
Plato's Critias tells a story he says came from Solon, who heard it from priests at Saïs in Egypt. Nine thousand years before, beyond the Pillars of Heracles, lay the island of Atlantis, larger than Libya and Asia together. Poseidon had fathered its kings on the mortal Cleito, and ringed her hill with alternating bands of sea and land. Its ten kings ruled a great empire from a city of concentric harbours, with temples covered in silver and orichalcum.

As the divine strain in the kings thinned, they grew greedy and marched to enslave the Mediterranean, and ancient Athens alone turned them back. Then, in a single dreadful day and night of earthquakes and floods, the Athenian army sank into the earth and Atlantis was swallowed by the sea, leaving only an impassable shoal of mud. The Critias breaks off just as Zeus gathers the gods to pass sentence.
versions.caveat: Most scholars regard Atlantis as Plato's own invention, a philosophical parable rather than a transmitted myth.

image.caption: Athanasius Kircher's map of Atlantis, Mundus Subterraneus, 1664

versions.title: The Sea Takes Dvārakā
versions.teaser: As Arjuna leads the survivors out, the ocean floods Krishna's city.
versions.text:
Dvārakā is Krishna's city on the western sea. After thirty-six years, a curse falls on his people, the Yādavas: drunk at a seaside festival, they quarrel and kill one another with reeds that have turned into iron clubs. Krishna's brother Balarama leaves his body, and Krishna himself is killed by a hunter's arrow as he sits in meditation.

Arjuna comes to lead the survivors, the women, children and old men, out of the city. As the last of them pass through the gates, the ocean, which Krishna had held back, rushes in. The sea floods the streets and palaces behind them, and they watch it cover the city as they go. Worse follows: on the road, a band of herdsmen attacks the convoy, and Arjuna finds that his great bow Gāṇḍīva has grown too heavy and his divine weapons will not come to mind. The age of heroes ends with its city under water.
versions.caveat: Claims that marine archaeology off modern Dwarka confirms the epic city are disputed.

versions.title: The Lake at Liyang
versions.teaser: Blood on the city gate: the kind old woman runs, and the city sinks.
versions.text:
The Huainanzi mentions in passing that the city of Liyang ‘became a lake in a single night’. Its commentator Gao You tells the story behind it.

An old woman of Liyang was known for her kindness. Two passing scholars told her that the city was about to sink and become a lake; when she saw blood on the threshold of the east gate, she should run to the northern hills without looking back. From then on she went every day to look at the threshold. The gatekeeper asked what she was doing, and she told him. That evening, as a joke, he killed a chicken and smeared its blood on the gate. Next morning the old woman saw the blood and fled to the hills. Behind her the city sank, and a lake lay where it had been. The gatekeeper's prank had been, without his knowing it, the true sign.
sources: Gao You, commentary on the Huainanzi

versions.title: The Lowland Hundred
versions.teaser: Beneath Cardigan Bay lie drowned fields, and their bells still ring.
versions.text:
Cantre'r Gwaelod, the Lowland Hundred, was a rich country ruled by Gwyddno Garanhir, now lying under Cardigan Bay. The oldest witness is a poem in the Black Book of Carmarthen: ‘Seithenhin, stand forth and look upon the fury of the sea: it has covered Maes Gwyddno.’ The poem lays the blame on a maiden, cursing ‘the maiden who released it after the feast, the cupbearer of the well of the mighty sea’, as though the flood came from a spring left unguarded.

Later tradition tells it differently. The lowland was protected by dykes and sluices, and Seithennin, the keeper, got drunk at a feast and left the sluices open to a spring tide, drowning the whole country. At low tide, old walls and stumps of forest appear on the beaches of the bay, and people say that on quiet days the church bells of the drowned hundred can still be heard, a belief sung in ‘The Bells of Aberdovey’.
sources: Black Book of Carmarthen, ‘Boddi Maes Gwyddno’
versions.caveat: The drunken dyke-keeper version is attested only from the early modern period; the medieval poem is obscure and blames a well-maiden.

versions.title: The City of Ys
versions.teaser: A princess steals the key of the sea gates, and Ys drowns.
versions.text:
King Gradlon rules Ker-Ys, a splendid city on the bay of Douarnenez, protected from the sea by walls and a great gate whose key never leaves him. His daughter Dahut is beautiful, wilful and wicked. In the fullest versions she steals the key from her sleeping father for a lover, who is the Devil in disguise, and the gates are opened to the tide.

The sea pours in. Gradlon mounts his horse and flees with Dahut behind him, the waves at the horse's hooves. The holy abbot Gwénolé calls out that he must cast off the sinner he carries, and Dahut falls or is thrown into the flood, which stops at once. Gradlon founds a new capital at Quimper, where his statue rides between the cathedral's spires. Dahut becomes a mari-morgan, a sea-woman luring sailors, and fishermen say the bells of Ys ring beneath the bay.
sources: Albert Le Grand, Vies des saints de la Bretagne Armorique (1636)
Hersart de La Villemarqué, Barzaz Breiz (1839)
versions.caveat: The story is first recorded in Christian hagiography and was heavily shaped by 19th-century collectors, whose authenticity is debated.

image.caption: The Flight of King Gradlon, by Évariste-Vital Luminais, c. 1884

versions.title: Invisible Kitezh
versions.teaser: To escape Batu's army, a holy city vanishes into Lake Svetloyar.
versions.text:
Great Kitezh, built by the prince Georgy Vsevolodovich on the shore of Lake Svetloyar, is a city of white churches in the forests beyond the Volga. When Batu Khan's army invades Rus in 1238, it advances on Kitezh. The city does not fight. By God's will it becomes invisible and sinks beneath the lake, and the invaders find only water and forest.

Kitezh is not destroyed but hidden, and it will stay hidden until the end of time. Only the pure in heart can find it: pilgrims to the lake say that on quiet nights they hear its bells ringing and the singing of its services, and see the lights of processions far beneath the surface. Old Believers, who saw themselves as the faithful remnant of a fallen church, cherished the legend above all.
sources: Kitezh Chronicle (Kitezhsky letopisets), Old Believer text
versions.caveat: The written legend is a Christian text surviving in 18th-century Old Believer copies; the Mongol-era setting is legendary, not historical.

image.caption: The Sunken City, by Konstantin Gorbatov, 1933

concepts.summary: Many traditions treat poetry not as a skill but as a visitation: something poured into the poet from outside, by Muses, gods, a stolen mead or a burning drop from a cauldron. Others place its origin in a single overwhelming moment of feeling. The idea is natural wherever verse carries memory, law and praise, and where a poet's words feel as though they arrive unbidden. The Indo-European traditions here may share some inherited language about poetic inspiration, a point comparativists have long argued, but the Japanese and Sanskrit stories show that the idea does not need a common ancestor.

versions.title: The Muses on Helicon
versions.teaser: Nine goddesses mock a shepherd, hand him a laurel staff, and breathe song.
versions.text:
Hesiod tells how his vocation began. He was pasturing lambs under holy Helicon when the Muses, daughters of Zeus, came to him and spoke first with scorn: ‘Shepherds of the wilds, base things of shame, mere bellies! We know how to tell many falsehoods that seem like truth, and we know, when we wish, how to utter true things.’

Then they plucked a staff for him, a branch of flourishing laurel, and breathed into him a divine voice so that he might celebrate the things that shall be and the things that were. They told him to sing of the blessed gods who live forever, and always to sing of the Muses themselves first and last. The Theogony that follows is presented as that gift. The Muses' boast is the uncomfortable part: the goddesses who inspire the poet admit that they are quite capable of lying through him.

image.caption: Hesiod and the Muse, by Gustave Moreau, 1891

versions.title: Grief Becomes the Śloka
versions.teaser: A hunter shoots a courting bird, and the sage's curse comes out in metre.
versions.text:
The sage Vālmīki goes down to the river Tamasā to bathe. In the woods he watches a pair of krauñca birds, curlews or cranes, absorbed in each other. A Niṣāda hunter shoots the male, and it falls bleeding while its mate cries out over it.

Filled with pity, Vālmīki speaks a curse: ‘Hunter, may you never find rest for endless years, since you killed one of this pair of krauñcas in the midst of its love.’ Only afterwards does he notice what he has said. The words fell into four equal quarters of eight syllables, fit to be sung to the lute. Since it was born of śoka, grief, he says, let it be called śloka. Then the god Brahmā appears and tells him to use this new metre to tell the whole story of Rāma. So Vālmīki becomes the ādikavi, the first poet, and the Rāmāyaṇa the first poem.

versions.title: Eightfold Clouds of Izumo
versions.teaser: A storm god builds a house for his bride and speaks the first waka.
versions.text:
After killing the eight-headed serpent, the storm god Susanoo marries Kushinada-hime and looks for a place in Izumo to build their palace. At Suga he says that his heart feels refreshed, and as he builds, clouds rise up around the place. He sings: ‘Eightfold clouds rise; / Izumo's eightfold fence / to enclose my wife / I build an eightfold fence, / oh, that eightfold fence!’

Two centuries later, Ki no Tsurayuki's preface to the Kokinshū made this song the start of Japanese poetry. Poetry, he writes, takes the human heart as its seed and grows into countless leaves of words; it moves heaven and earth without effort, stirs unseen spirits to pity, softens the bond of men and women and calms fierce warriors. It began when heaven and earth began: in heaven with Shitateru-hime, and on earth with Susanoo, with whom the thirty-one-syllable form first appears.
sources: Kokinshū, Japanese preface by Ki no Tsurayuki (c. 905)

versions.title: The Mead of Poetry
versions.teaser: Brewed from a murdered sage's blood, stolen by Odin in eagle form.
versions.text:
When the Æsir and Vanir make peace, they seal it by spitting into a vat, and from that spittle they make Kvasir, so wise that no one can ask him a question he cannot answer. Two dwarfs, Fjalar and Galar, murder him and mix his blood with honey in three vessels, Óðrerir, Boðn and Són. Whoever drinks the mead becomes a poet or a scholar.

The mead passes to the giant Suttungr, who hides it inside a mountain with his daughter Gunnlöð as guard. Odin, calling himself Bölverkr, has a hole bored into the rock, slips through as a snake, and spends three nights with Gunnlöð. For each night she gives him one drink, and with three drinks he empties all three vessels. He flies home as an eagle, Suttungr in pursuit, and spits the mead into vessels set out by the gods. Some he lets fall behind him, and that share, Snorri says, goes to bad poets.

image.caption: Odin as an eagle spits out the mead of poetry; Icelandic manuscript SÁM 66, 18th century

versions.title: Three Drops from Ceridwen's Cauldron
versions.teaser: A kitchen boy tastes the brew of wisdom and is reborn as Taliesin.
versions.text:
Ceridwen, a wise woman of Llyn Tegid, has a son so ugly that she resolves to make him wise instead, and sets a cauldron of inspiration boiling for a year and a day. The boy Gwion Bach is set to stir it. At the end, three drops leap out and scald his finger; he puts it in his mouth and at once knows everything, including that Ceridwen will kill him. The cauldron bursts, its remaining brew now poison.

The chase through a series of shapes, told on the shapeshifters page, ends when Ceridwen, as a black hen, swallows him as a grain of wheat. Nine months later she bears him again and, unable to kill so beautiful a child, sets him adrift in a leather bag. Elffin finds him in a fishing weir and names him Taliesin, ‘radiant brow’, and the infant answers in verse. The brew meant to make an ugly boy wise has made the chief of bards instead, and poems in the Book of Taliesin speak of Ceridwen's cauldron as a source of awen, poetic inspiration.
sources: Hanes Taliesin, in the chronicle of Elis Gruffydd (16th century)
versions.caveat: The prose tale is recorded only in the sixteenth century, though earlier Welsh poems allude to Ceridwen's cauldron and Taliesin's transformations.

concepts.summary: Writing is a late invention, and many cultures remembered it as a single act by a god, king or culture hero: a messenger's burden transferred to clay, a sage copying bird tracks, a god taking up runes in agony. The stories often carry a worry alongside the wonder, that writing weakens memory, disturbs the spirits, or belongs to the powerful. Since scripts demonstrably spread by borrowing, some of these legends preserve real history (Herodotus is right about the Phoenicians), while others are independent attempts to explain an art that seemed, to those who first used it, close to magic.

versions.title: Words on Clay
versions.teaser: The message grew too long, so the king of Uruk wrote it down.
versions.text:
Enmerkar, lord of Uruk, wants gold, silver and lapis lazuli from the distant city of Aratta, beyond seven mountains, to adorn the temple of the goddess Inana. He sends a messenger again and again, and the two kings trade threats, boasts and riddles, each answer longer than the last.

At last the message becomes too much: the messenger's mouth is heavy, and he cannot repeat it. So Enmerkar pats a lump of clay and sets the words upon it like a tablet. ‘Before that day,’ the poem says, ‘there had been no putting of words on clay; now, with the sun rising, so it was.’ The messenger carries the tablet across the mountains. The lord of Aratta takes the clay and looks at it. The spoken words have become wedges, and he frowns at them. The first reader in literature is thus a baffled one.
sources: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta (Sumerian)

image.caption: Tablet with proto-cuneiform writing, Uruk III period, late 4th millennium BCE, Louvre

versions.title: Thoth's Gift and Thamus's Doubt
versions.teaser: The ibis-headed scribe of the gods offers letters; the king has reservations.
versions.text:
Thoth, Djehuty, is the scribe of the gods, the ibis- or baboon-formed lord of the medu netjer, the ‘divine words’, as Egyptians called their hieroglyphs. He records the verdict when the heart of the dead is weighed, reckons time by the moon, and is the patron of every scribe.

Greek writers knew him as the inventor of letters, and Plato gives the most famous version. Theuth brings his inventions to King Thamus at Thebes: number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, draughts and dice, and above all writing, which he calls a remedy for memory and wisdom. Thamus answers that it is the opposite. Writing will produce forgetfulness in those who learn it, since they will trust external marks instead of remembering from within, and they will seem wise without being so. It is a remedy for reminding, not for memory.
versions.caveat: Egyptian texts make Thoth the lord of writing, but the dialogue with Thamus is Plato's Greek framing, not an attested Egyptian myth.

image.file: File:The judgement of the dead in the presence of Osiris.jpg
image.caption: Ibis-headed Thoth records the weighing of the heart; Papyrus of Hunefer, c. 1275 BCE

versions.title: Cadmus Brings the Letters
versions.teaser: Phoenicians with Cadmus bring the alphabet, and Greeks reshape its letters.
versions.text:
Herodotus explains the Greek alphabet historically. The Phoenicians who came to Boeotia with Cadmus, the founder of Thebes, brought many arts with them, and above all letters, which the Greeks had not had before. At first they wrote exactly as the Phoenicians did; over time they changed both the sound and the shape of the letters. The Ionians, who learned them first, went on calling them phoinikeia, ‘Phoenician things’.

Herodotus adds that he has seen such Cadmean letters himself, engraved on three tripods in the temple of Ismenian Apollo at Thebes, mostly resembling Ionian letters, and he quotes the verses on them. He notes too that the Ionians call papyrus scrolls ‘skins’, from a time when they wrote on goat and sheep hides. Other Greeks credited Palamedes, or Prometheus, with the invention. The legend is unusually close to the truth: the Greek alphabet really was adapted from the Phoenician.

versions.title: Cangjie and the Weeping Ghosts
versions.teaser: A sage reads bird tracks; heaven rains grain and ghosts wail.
versions.text:
Cangjie, remembered as a scribe of the Yellow Emperor, is the inventor of Chinese characters. The Xunzi already names him: many people in antiquity were fond of writing, but only Cangjie's was handed down, because he was single-minded.

The Huainanzi records the cosmic response. When Cangjie created writing, Heaven rained down millet, and the ghosts wept all night. The line was read in various ways: the ghosts wept because their secrets could now be written down, or because people would abandon farming for the clever business of documents. Xu Shen, in the postface to his dictionary, gives the method: Cangjie observed the tracks of birds and animals, saw that their patterns could be told apart, and created the first written signs. Later portraits give him four eyes, the better to see such patterns.

image.caption: Four-eyed Cangjie, from an album of portraits of sages, National Palace Museum

versions.title: Odin Takes Up the Runes
versions.teaser: Nine nights on the windy tree, wounded, unfed, then the runes.
versions.text:
In Hávamál Odin himself speaks: ‘I know that I hung on a windy tree nine full nights, wounded with a spear and given to Odin, myself to myself, on that tree of which no one knows from what roots it rises. They gave me no bread, nor drink from a horn. I peered down; I took up the runes, screaming I took them, and I fell back from there.’

The poem goes on to speak of runes painted by the great sage and carved by the ruler of the gods, and of the questions every rune-user must be able to answer: how to carve, how to read, how to stain, how to test, how to ask, how to sacrifice. The runes here are more than an alphabet; the word rún also means ‘secret’. Odin does not so much invent them as win them from the depths, at the price of a sacrifice of himself to himself.
versions.caveat: Hávamál presents Odin as winning the runes rather than inventing them, and the runic script is far older than the poem.

versions.title: Ogma's Letters
versions.teaser: A god skilled in speech invents ogham and writes a warning in birch.
versions.text:
The Auraicept na nÉces, the medieval Irish ‘Scholars' Primer’, names the inventor of ogham, the script of notches carved along the edges of standing stones: Ogma, son of Elatha, a man well skilled in speech and in poetry. He devised it as proof of his ingenuity, the primer says, and so that it should be a speech belonging to the learned alone, apart from rustics and herdsmen.

The first thing ever written in ogham was seven letter b's, carved on a birch rod, a warning sent to the god Lug: his wife would be carried off into the otherworld unless she was guarded. The letters bear the names of trees, beith ‘birch’ for b and luis for l, and the whole system is taught as a kind of forest. In the same primer Irish itself is said to have been assembled from the best of all languages after the confusion at Babel.
versions.caveat: This is the learned lore of medieval Irish grammarians, recorded long after ogham inscriptions were first cut in the early centuries CE.

image.caption: Ogham stone at Tullaherin, County Kilkenny

versions.title: The Demons Teach Tahmuras
versions.teaser: Defeated demons buy their lives by teaching the king thirty scripts.
versions.text:
Tahmuras, the third king of the world in the Shāhnāmeh, is called Dīvband, ‘Binder of Demons’. He tames the beasts, spins wool, and by spells binds Ahriman himself and rides him like a horse around the world.

The demons rebel and gather a great army of demons and sorcerers. Tahmuras meets them with his heavy mace, binds two-thirds of them by magic and strikes down the rest. Bound and battered, they beg for their lives, offering in exchange a new art. He spares them, and they teach him to write: not one script but nearly thirty, Firdawsī says, among them Rūmī, Arabic, Persian, Sogdian, Chinese and Pahlavi. In this telling, writing is not a gift of heaven at all. It is ransom taken from the powers of darkness, and a king's hard-won spoil.

image.caption: Tahmuras Defeats the Divs, from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, c. 1525

concepts.summary: Song and instruments are among the oldest human arts, and many cultures credit their first making to a god, a trickster or a culture hero. The details are wonderfully local: a tortoise shell, a pike's jawbone, bamboo cut to the call of a phoenix, a stamping dance on an upturned tub. Often music is fetched or stolen from elsewhere, from the sky, the sea or the house of the Sun, or it arrives with the arts of civilization. These are almost certainly independent inventions; what they share is the sense that music is too powerful to have been merely thought up.

versions.title: Jubal, Father of the Lyre
versions.teaser: In Cain's line, one brother herds, one forges, one plays.
versions.text:
Genesis gives the origin of music a single verse, in the genealogy of Cain. Lamech takes two wives, Adah and Zillah. Adah bears Jabal, the ancestor of those who live in tents and keep livestock, and his brother Jubal, ‘the father of all who handle the lyre and the pipe’, the kinnor and the ugab. Zillah bears Tubal-cain, who forges every kind of tool of bronze and iron.

The arrangement is telling. Herding, metalwork and music arrive together, a set of arts of civilization, and they come not from heaven but from a human family, the descendants of the first murderer. The same passage preserves Lamech's savage song to his wives, boasting that he has killed a man for wounding him. Music, in this oldest biblical account, is simply one of the things people learned to do after leaving the garden.

versions.title: Hermes and the Tortoise
versions.teaser: A day-old god turns a tortoise into a lyre and charms Apollo.
versions.text:
Hermes is born at dawn in a cave on Mount Cyllene; by midday he is playing the lyre, and by evening he has stolen Apollo's cattle. Stepping out of the cave, he meets a tortoise waddling through the grass and greets it as a lucky find. He carries it inside, scoops out its flesh with a chisel of grey iron, cuts reed stalks to length, stretches oxhide over the shell, fits arms and a crossbar, and strings it with seven strings of sheep gut. He tries it out and sings of Zeus and Maia and his own birth.

When Apollo tracks down the thief, furious, Hermes plays for him, and Apollo is enchanted; he would give the fifty cows for the music alone. So Hermes hands over the lyre and keeps the herds, and makes himself shepherd's pipes instead. The god of music thus receives his instrument secondhand, from a baby thief.

versions.title: Ling Lun's Bamboo Pipes
versions.teaser: The Yellow Emperor's musician tunes twelve pipes to the phoenix's call.
versions.text:
The Lüshi chunqiu tells how the Yellow Emperor ordered Ling Lun to make pitch-pipes. Ling Lun travelled west, beyond Daxia to the north side of Ruanyu, and took bamboo from the valley of Xiexi, choosing stems with hollows of even thickness. He cut a length between two nodes and blew it, and its note became the huangzhong, the ‘yellow bell’, the foundation pitch.

Then, below the mountain of Ruanyu, he listened to the singing of the phoenixes, male and female, and cut twelve pipes: six to match the calls of the male bird, and six those of the female, so that the twelve pitches of music were set in their places. With these, the Yellow Emperor had bells cast to match the pitches. Music here is less composed than discovered, a set of intervals already present in nature and the cosmos that the sage has only to measure accurately.

versions.title: The Fifth Veda
versions.teaser: Brahmā takes song from the Sāmaveda and makes a Veda for everyone.
versions.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra, the great Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music, opens with its own origin. In the Tretā age, when the world had grown full of desire and grief, the gods led by Indra asked Brahmā for a diversion to be both seen and heard, one that could be shared by all classes, since the four Vedas might not be heard by śūdras.

Brahmā meditated and made a fifth Veda, the Nāṭyaveda. He took recitation from the Ṛgveda, song from the Sāmaveda, gesture and acting from the Yajurveda, and emotional flavour, rasa, from the Atharvaveda. He gave it to the sage Bharata and his hundred sons. The first performance, at Indra's banner festival, showed the gods defeating the demons; the demons in the audience took offence and froze the actors' speech and movement, until Indra beat them off with the banner pole and Viśvakarman built a protected playhouse.

versions.title: Uzume's Dance at the Rock Cave
versions.teaser: A goddess stamps on an upturned tub, and laughter brings back the sun.
versions.text:
Offended by her brother Susanoo, the sun goddess Amaterasu shuts herself in the Rock Cave of Heaven, and the world falls into darkness. The eight hundred myriad gods gather at the cave mouth. They set long-crying birds to crow, forge a mirror, string curved jewels, and hang them on a sakaki tree.

Then Ame-no-Uzume ties up her sleeves with a vine, crowns herself with leaves, takes bamboo leaves in her hand, and sets a tub upside down before the cave. She stamps on it until it resounds, falls into divine possession, bares her breasts and pushes her skirt down. The gods roar with laughter. Amaterasu, puzzled that anyone can laugh in the dark, opens the door a crack; she sees her own brightness in the mirror, and a strong god pulls her out. The court performers called Sarume traced their descent from Uzume, and her dance is remembered as the origin of kagura, sacred music and dance.

image.caption: Origin of the Cave Door Dance (Iwato Kagura), by Shunsai Toshimasa, 1889

versions.title: Music Fetched from the Sun
versions.teaser: Wind crosses the sea to steal musicians from the House of the Sun.
versions.text:
The earth has no music, so Tezcatlipoca sends the Wind to the House of the Sun to fetch singers and instruments. The Wind goes to the edge of the sea and calls up the creatures of the waters to make a bridge for him, and crosses to the Sun's house.

There the Sun's musicians play and sing. The Sun sees the Wind coming and warns them: whoever answers his call will have to go with him. The Wind begins to sing to them in a sweet voice, and some of the musicians cannot resist answering. Those he carries back across the sea to the earth, and from them come the songs and dances with which people have honoured the gods ever since. It is a theft story with no violence in it at all; the Wind simply sings better than the Sun can forbid.
sources: Gerónimo de Mendieta, Historia eclesiástica indiana, Book 2
versions.caveat: The story survives only in a Franciscan friar's late 16th-century summary, not in a Nahuatl text.

versions.title: The Pike-Bone Kantele
versions.teaser: Väinämöinen builds a harp from a giant pike's jawbone, and all creation weeps.
versions.text:
On the voyage to Pohjola, Väinämöinen's boat sticks fast on the shoulders of a giant pike. Lemminkäinen and Ilmarinen try to kill it and fail; Väinämöinen cuts it in two. From its jawbone he makes a kantele, the Finnish zither, with pegs from its teeth and strings from the hair of Hiisi's gelding.

No one else can play it, but when Väinämöinen sits down to play, the whole world comes to listen. Squirrels leap from branch to branch to hear him, lynxes and wolves come out of the forest, the bear climbs the fence, eagles leave their nests, and the fish of the sea and Ahti, the sea's master, rise to the surface. Everyone who hears him weeps, and at last Väinämöinen weeps too. His tears roll down to the sea and become blue pearls, which a duck dives to bring back. When the kantele is later lost at sea, he makes a new one of birch.
versions.caveat: The Kalevala is Lönnrot's 19th-century compilation from traditional songs, whose episodes he combined and ordered himself.

image.caption: Väinämöinen Playing the Kantele, sketch by Robert Wilhelm Ekman, Finnish National Gallery

concepts.summary: Many early states explained royal power by bringing it down from above. Kingship descends from heaven to a first city, a divine grandson steps down onto a mountain, a glory attaches itself to rightful kings and deserts the unworthy, or a mandate is granted and withdrawn by Heaven itself. The idea is an obvious answer to an obvious political problem, the need to make one person's rule seem natural and permanent, and it arises independently wherever kings do. What varies instructively is whether the gift is permanent, as a bloodline, or conditional, as a mandate that can be lost.

versions.title: The Lowering of Kingship
versions.teaser: Kingship comes down to Eridu, is washed away, and comes down again.
versions.text:
The Sumerian King List begins: ‘When kingship was lowered from heaven, the kingship was in Eridu. In Eridu, Alulim became king; he ruled for 28,800 years.’ The kingship moves from city to city, eight kings in five cities ruling for a total of 241,200 years. ‘Then the flood swept over. After the flood had swept over, when kingship was lowered from heaven, the kingship was in Kish.’

Kingship here is a single thing, an office, not a family. It sits in one city at a time and is ‘carried off’ to another when a city is defeated, so that the whole of Sumerian history becomes the travels of one heavenly gift. The Akkadian myth of Etana adds a picture of the time before: the sceptre, the crown and the shepherd's staff lay before the god Anu in heaven, until the gods sent kingship down and made Etana of Kish the first shepherd of the people.

image.file: File:Weld-Blundell Prism, initial paragraph about rule of Alulim in Eridu for 28800 years.jpg
image.caption: Opening lines of the Sumerian King List on the Weld-Blundell Prism, c. 1800 BCE

versions.title: The Living Horus
versions.teaser: Gods ruled Egypt first; every pharaoh sits on Horus's throne.
versions.text:
Egyptian lists of kings begin with gods. The Turin King List, a papyrus of the thirteenth century BCE, opens with divine rulers, among them Ptah, Ra, Shu, Geb, Osiris, Seth and Horus, followed by spirits and demigods, before the human king Menes. Manetho, writing in Greek a thousand years later, gives the same order.

Every pharaoh inherits that throne. The king's first title is his Horus name: he is the living Horus, the son who avenged his murdered father Osiris and won the kingship of Egypt from his uncle Seth. The Contendings of Horus and Seth tells that contest as an eighty-year lawsuit before the gods, full of trickery and indignity, ending when the tribunal awards the throne to Horus. From the Old Kingdom the king is also ‘son of Ra’, and in the famous seated statue of Khafre, the falcon Horus spreads his wings behind the king's head.
sources: The Contendings of Horus and Seth (Papyrus Chester Beatty I)

image.caption: Seated statue of Khafre with the Horus falcon behind his head, 4th Dynasty, Egyptian Museum, Cairo

versions.title: The Mandate of Heaven
versions.teaser: Heaven gives the right to rule, and takes it back from tyrants.
versions.text:
The Shang royal house traced itself to heaven. A hymn in the Book of Songs says: ‘Heaven commanded the dark bird to descend and give birth to Shang.’ But the Zhou, who conquered the Shang around 1046 BCE, needed a different doctrine, and they made one of the most durable ideas in Chinese political thought.

In the speeches of the early Zhou preserved in the Book of Documents, Heaven confers its mandate, tianming, on a ruler, but not forever. The last Shang kings lost it through drunkenness, cruelty and neglect of the people, and Heaven transferred it to King Wen and King Wu of Zhou. The king is the Son of Heaven, but he holds his office on condition of virtue, and floods, famines and revolts can be read as signs that the mandate is slipping. Mencius later quotes an old saying: ‘Heaven sees as my people see; Heaven hears as my people hear.’

versions.title: The Royal Glory
versions.teaser: A radiant glory rests on true kings, and flies from liars as a bird.
versions.text:
The Zamyād Yasht praises the kavaēm xᵛarənah, the royal glory created by Ahura Mazda, which attaches itself to the rightful rulers of the world one after another: Haoshyangha, Takhma Urupi, and Yima the splendid, under whom there was neither heat nor cold, old age nor death.

But when Yima begins to lie, the glory leaves him visibly, flying off in the form of a bird. It departs three times and is caught by others: by Mithra, by the dragon-slayer Thraētaona and by the hero Kərəsāspa. Yima, bereft, wanders confounded on the earth. The Turanian Franrasyan strips off his clothes and dives three times into the Vourukasha sea to seize the glory for himself, and each time it slips away. In later Persian, as farr, it becomes the halo of legitimate kingship in the Shāhnāmeh, and Sasanian kings are shown receiving their diadem from the god himself.

image.caption: Ardashir I receives the ring of kingship from Ahura Mazda; Sasanian relief at Naqsh-e Rustam, 3rd century CE

versions.title: A King Made of Gods
versions.teaser: In a kingless, frightened world, the Lord makes a king from eight deities.
versions.text:
The Laws of Manu explain why there are kings. When the world was without a king and everyone scattered in fear, the Lord created the king for the protection of the whole world. He made him from eternal particles of eight gods: Indra, the Wind, Yama, the Sun, Fire, Varuṇa, the Moon and Kubera, lord of wealth. Because he is formed from these lords of the gods, the king outshines all beings in splendour, and like the sun he burns eyes and hearts, so no one can look at him directly.

Even a child king, Manu warns, must not be despised as a mere mortal, for he is a great deity in human form. The Purāṇas tell of Pṛthu, consecrated as the first king after the sages killed the wicked Vena. Pṛthu chases the earth, who has fled in the form of a cow, until she agrees to be milked and to give food to all creatures again.

versions.title: The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
versions.teaser: The sun goddess sends her grandson down with a mirror, jewels and sword.
versions.text:
The land below, the Central Land of Reed Plains, has been pacified, and Amaterasu and Takamimusubi send her grandson Ninigi down from the Plain of High Heaven to rule it. She gives him the curved jewels and the mirror that had drawn her out of the Rock Cave, and the sword Kusanagi that Susanoo found in the tail of the serpent, telling him to regard the mirror as her own spirit. The ancestors of five clans go with him, and the earthly god Sarutahiko meets him at the crossroads of heaven to guide him.

Ninigi pushes through the eightfold clouds and descends onto the peak of Takachiho in Himuka. The Nihon Shoki gives Amaterasu's command in a variant: this land is the land our descendants shall rule; go and govern it; the prosperity of the heavenly succession shall be as endless as heaven and earth. His great-grandson becomes Jimmu, the first emperor, and the three regalia remain the imperial treasures.

image.caption: Ninigi and his retinue descend to earth, illustration published 1911

versions.title: The Golden Staff
versions.teaser: The Sun sends his children with a rod that sinks where Cuzco must stand.
versions.text:
Garcilaso de la Vega, son of a Spanish captain and an Inca princess, heard this from his mother's uncle. Long ago people lived like wild beasts, without houses, clothing or farming. The Sun, pitying them, sent his son and daughter, Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, to earth at Lake Titicaca to teach them to live as human beings.

He gave them a golden rod, less than a yard long and two fingers thick. Wherever they went, they were to thrust it into the ground; where it sank in at a single blow, they were to found their court. They travelled north, and at the hill of Huanacauri, above the valley of Cuzco, the rod sank in and disappeared. There they called the people together. Manco Cápac taught the men to farm and irrigate, and Mama Ocllo taught the women to spin and weave. Every Inca after them was a child of the Sun.
sources: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas I.15–16 (1609)
versions.caveat: This is one of several colonial-era Inca origin accounts; others have the Ayar siblings emerge from a cave at Pacaritambo.

image.caption: Manco Cápac, colonial-era portrait

versions.title: Oduduwa at Ile-Ife
versions.teaser: Let down by a chain from heaven, the first king spreads the earth.
versions.text:
In the beginning there is only water below the sky. In the widespread Ife tradition, Olodumare, the supreme god, sends a divine messenger down by a chain with a little earth and a hen, in many tellings a five-toed hen. In many versions Obatala is sent first but drinks palm wine and falls asleep, so Oduduwa takes the materials and goes down in his place. He scatters the earth on the water, sets the hen upon it, and the hen scratches and spreads the earth in every direction until dry land lies at Ile-Ife, the place where the earth was spread.

Oduduwa becomes the first king at Ife, and his descendants go out to found the other Yoruba kingdoms, including Oyo, carrying their right to wear the beaded crown. Yoruba obas trace their legitimacy to that descent, and Ile-Ife is still revered as the cradle of the kingship.
sources: Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (1921)
versions.caveat: Yoruba traditions differ, notably on the rivalry of Oduduwa and Obatala, and Johnson also records a version in which Oduduwa migrates from the east.

concepts.summary: An earthquake is the most unnerving of natural events: the one thing that should never move, moves. Myths explain it with a living cause beneath or behind the ground: a god's footsteps, an elephant shifting its load, a bound criminal writhing, an unborn child stirring in his mother, a giant catfish thrashing under a stone. Many traditions also turn quakes into signs, of divine presence or anger. The variety is great and the resemblances general, which points to independent invention; the shared logic is that the earth moves because something alive moves it.

versions.title: The Earth Trembled
versions.teaser: The quake is the footstep of the God who comes from Seir.
versions.text:
In the Hebrew Bible there is no monster under the ground. The earthquake is a sign of the God of Israel on the move. When he descends on Sinai, the mountain is wrapped in smoke and the whole mountain quakes greatly. The Song of Deborah remembers his coming from the south: ‘Lord, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the fields of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured, the mountains quaked before the Lord.’ A psalm says that the earth reeled and rocked, and the foundations of the mountains trembled, because he was angry.

A real earthquake became a date: the prophet Amos spoke ‘two years before the earthquake’, and Zechariah, centuries later, recalls how the people fled it in the days of King Uzziah. For Isaiah the final judgment looks like the last quake of all, the earth staggering like a drunkard and swaying like a hut.

versions.title: The Earth-Shaker
versions.teaser: Poseidon shakes the ground so hard that Hades leaps from his throne.
versions.text:
Poseidon's oldest titles call him Enosichthon and Ennosigaios, ‘Earth-shaker’, as well as lord of the sea. In the Iliad, when the gods take sides and go to war, Zeus thunders from above and Poseidon shakes the boundless earth and the steep summits of the mountains below: all the slopes of Ida tremble, and the city of Troy and the Greek ships. Beneath the ground, Hades, lord of the dead, leaps from his throne in terror and cries out, afraid that Poseidon will split the earth open and lay bare to gods and mortals the dank and dreadful halls that even the gods hate.

The Greeks acted on the belief. When an earthquake struck a Spartan army invading Argos, Xenophon reports, the soldiers struck up a hymn to Poseidon. And when the city of Helike sank into the Corinthian Gulf in 373 BCE, it was remembered as Poseidon's punishment for an outrage at his shrine.

versions.title: The Elephant Beneath the East
versions.teaser: When the world-elephant shifts its weary head, the earth shakes.
versions.text:
King Sagara's sixty thousand sons, searching for a stolen sacrificial horse, dig down through the whole earth, tearing through its layers and killing the creatures who live there. Deep below, in the eastern quarter, they come upon a great elephant, Virūpākṣa, as large as a mountain, holding the earth, with its mountains and forests, on his head.

The Rāmāyaṇa explains what they are seeing. When the great elephant grows tired and moves his head to rest it, the earth shakes: that is an earthquake. The princes walk round him respectfully and dig on, and at the other quarters they find his fellows, the world-elephants who bear the earth at the south, west and north. The digging does not end well: they find the horse grazing near the sage Kapila, accuse him of theft, and are burned to ashes by his gaze. Only the descent of the Ganges, generations later, can purify them.

versions.title: Earthquake Is Tricked
versions.teaser: The mountain-toppler eats a roast bird coated in earth, and loses his strength.
versions.text:
Seven Macaw, the false sun, has two sons as boastful as himself. Zipacna makes mountains; Cabracan, whose name means ‘Earthquake’, knocks them down, shaking the great mountains and the small ones whenever he stamps his feet. Heart of Sky sends the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, to deal with him.

The Twins meet Cabracan and tell him about a mountain in the east so tall that it rises above all the others. He cannot bear it and demands to be shown the way. As they walk, the Twins shoot birds with their blowguns and roast one for him, but they coat it in white earth. Cabracan eats it hungrily. When they reach the mountain, he has no strength left: the earth he swallowed has weakened him. The Twins tie his hands and feet, throw him to the ground, and bury him. The shaker of mountains is himself put underground.

versions.title: Sigyn's Bowl
versions.teaser: Each time Loki's wife empties her bowl of venom, the earth shakes.
versions.text:
The binding of Loki after Baldr's death is told on the bound-one page; here the point is what happens afterwards, in the cave. Loki lies across three stones, tied with the entrails of his son, and above his face the giantess Skaði has hung a venomous snake so that its poison drips on him.

He is not left entirely alone. His wife Sigyn stands beside him holding a bowl under the dripping venom. Hers is the only kindness in the story, and it cannot last. When the bowl is full she must turn away to empty it, and in that moment the poison falls on Loki's face. He writhes so violently against his bonds that the whole earth shakes, and that, Snorri says, is what people call an earthquake.

Every tremor marks a brief absence: a woman carrying a full bowl away and coming back. It will go on until Ragnarök, when all bonds break.

image.caption: Loki and Sigyn, by Mårten Eskil Winge, 1863

versions.title: Rūaumoko Stirs
versions.teaser: The unborn youngest son of Earth shifts inside her, and the ground trembles.
versions.text:
Rangi the sky and Papa the earth lay locked together until their children forced them apart, and the sky has wept for his wife ever since. In the account George Grey published, Rūaumoko, the youngest of their children, was still unborn at the separation. He remained within his mother's body, where he is still.

When he moves or turns in her, the earth quakes, and his restlessness is also the heat of the earth and its volcanoes. In some tellings, the sons of Papa turned her face downward so that she and Rangi would not have to see each other's grief, and Rūaumoko was left with her as a comfort and a source of warmth. The ground's tremors are therefore not an attack but a stirring in the womb, the movement of a god who has never been born.

versions.title: The Great Catfish
versions.teaser: A god pins a giant catfish under a stone; when he's away, it thrashes.
versions.text:
Beneath the ground lies a giant catfish, the ōnamazu. The god of Kashima Shrine, Takemikazuchi, keeps it pinned down with the kaname-ishi, the ‘keystone’, whose top can still be seen at the shrine; only a small part shows above the ground. When the god's attention lapses, the catfish thrashes, and the earth shakes.

After the great Ansei earthquake flattened much of Edo in 1855, the city was flooded with cheap woodblock prints of catfish, the namazu-e. In them the catfish is beaten by angry townspeople, begs forgiveness from the Kashima god, or is shown showering gold coins on the carpenters and plasterers who profited from rebuilding. The prints were at once talismans, satire and news: the quake as divine punishment, as a leveller of rich and poor, and as the working of a fish who needs watching.
sources: Cornelis Ouwehand, Namazu-e and Their Themes (1964)
versions.caveat: The catfish as cause of earthquakes is an Edo-period popular belief; earlier Japanese images placed a dragon or serpent beneath the land.

image.caption: The Kashima god and the keystone subdue the catfish; namazu-e print, c. 1855

concepts.summary: Some traditions imagine that the world's greatest danger will be cold: a winter so long and severe that it nearly ends life, and only those sheltered in a refuge will survive. The Iranian and Norse versions are strikingly alike, with a pre-announced winter and a chosen remnant in an enclosure or wood, and scholars have long debated whether this reflects shared Indo-European inheritance, later contact, or coincidence; none is proven. Nearby traditions offer related catastrophes of withheld growth or stolen light rather than frost, in which a divine grief or theft freezes the ordinary cycle of the seasons.

versions.title: Yima's Enclosure
versions.teaser: Warned of killing winters, Yima builds a refuge and gathers the best seed.
versions.text:
Yima is the first king, and under him the earth fills up with flocks and people until he must enlarge it three times. Then Ahura Mazda warns him: evil winters are coming upon the material world, bringing fierce, destroying frost. Snow will fall deep even on the highest mountains, and the cattle will perish, so that afterwards the mere footprint of a sheep will be a wonder.

Yima must build a vara, an enclosure, as long as a horse-course on every side. Into it he is to bring the seed of the best men and women, and of every kind of animal, plant and food, and fire, choosing the finest and admitting no one deformed, diseased or mean. Inside it he lays out streets and houses, with self-created lights. There the years pass like single days, and the people live in great happiness, waiting for the world outside to be ready again.

versions.title: Demeter's Barren Year
versions.teaser: Grieving for her daughter, the grain goddess lets nothing grow.
versions.text:
When Hades carries off Persephone, her mother Demeter searches the earth, then withdraws in grief and anger to her temple at Eleusis. The Homeric Hymn describes what follows as a most terrible and cruel year for mankind across the nourishing earth. The soil sends up no seed, for Demeter hides it. The oxen drag the curved ploughs over the fields in vain, and the white barley falls uselessly into the ground. She would have destroyed the whole race of mortals by famine, and robbed the gods of their sacrifices, had Zeus not noticed.

Zeus sends Hermes to bring Persephone back. But she has eaten a pomegranate seed below, so she must spend a portion of every year with Hades, and return each spring as flowers bloom. The world's growth thus depends on the comings and goings of a daughter, and the great barren year becomes the pattern for every year.
versions.caveat: The Hymn describes a famine, not a winter, and speaks of a third of the year below; reading it as the origin of winter is a later interpretation.

versions.title: Fimbulvetr
versions.teaser: Three winters with no summer between, and two humans hiding in a wood.
versions.text:
Before the end, Snorri says, comes the winter called Fimbulvetr, the ‘mighty winter’. Snow drives from every direction, the frosts are great and the winds sharp, and the sun gives no warmth. Three such winters come in succession with no summer between. Before them come three other winters of great wars across the world, when brothers kill each other for greed and no one spares father or son.

In Vafþrúðnismál, Odin asks the giant which of mankind will live when the famous Fimbulwinter has passed among men. The answer: Líf and Lífþrasir will hide in Hoddmímir's wood. They will eat the morning dew for food, and from them new generations will come. Völuspá adds its own omen: the sunshine turns black in the summers that follow, and the weather turns treacherous. The great winter is the prelude to Ragnarök, and the remnant who survive it seed the world that follows.
versions.caveat: The resemblance to Yima's enclosure has long been noted, but whether it reflects shared inheritance is unproven.

versions.title: Frost Without a Sun
versions.teaser: With sun, moon and fire stolen, frost settles on the crops of Kalevala.
versions.text:
When Louhi, mistress of Pohjola, hides the sun and moon inside a mountain and steals the fire from the hearths (the theft itself has its own page, under eclipses), the land of Kaleva is left not only dark but cold. The houses stand cold and cheerless, and Väinämöinen, setting out to find the lost fire, says that cold and darkness have long been his people's companions.

Even after the fire is recovered from the belly of a fish, the sun and moon stay hidden, and the cold deepens. Frost settles on the crops, the cattle die of hunger, even the birds sicken, and men and women perish in the cold and dark. The wise cannot tell when morning comes, and young and old debate how anyone can live without the sun.

The long night ends only when Ilmarinen begins forging fetters for Louhi, and she, frightened, lets the sun and moon go free.
versions.caveat: The cold here follows from the theft of the sun rather than being a foretold world-winter like Fimbulvetr, and the episode is Lönnrot's 19th-century arrangement of traditional songs.

concepts.summary: Not every mythology expects the world to end, but many do: by fire, flood, cosmic battle, falling stars or the return of the primeval waters. The endings mirror the beginnings, as creation is undone in its own order, and they often come at the close of a vast cycle of ages or as the final judgment of a god. The Norse, Iranian and Indic pictures have been compared since the nineteenth century, and some influence among Iranian, Jewish and later Christian apocalyptic is widely accepted, but many of the parallels here reflect a shared logic of time rather than a common source.

versions.title: Return to the Waters
versions.teaser: The creator will undo everything, leaving only himself as a serpent.
versions.text:
In a dialogue in the Book of the Dead, Osiris complains to the creator Atum about the underworld: it has no water, no air, it is deep and dark and endless. Atum consoles him and then speaks of the far future.

‘I shall destroy all that I have made,’ he says, ‘and this land will return into the Nun, into the flood, as it was in the beginning.’ Only Atum himself will remain, together with Osiris, after he has changed himself back into a serpent that no human knows and no god sees. It is one of the few Egyptian statements about the end of the world, and it is quiet and unnerving: no battle, no judgment, only the created world sinking back into the dark waters from which it rose, with the creator coiled in them as he was before the first day.

versions.title: The Day of the Lord
versions.teaser: The earth staggers like a drunkard; the sky rolls up like a scroll.
versions.text:
The prophets of Israel describe a coming ‘day of the Lord’ in images of cosmic undoing. Isaiah sees the Lord empty the earth and lay it waste: ‘the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble. The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart; the earth staggers like a drunkard and sways like a hut.’ Elsewhere the host of heaven rots away, the skies roll up like a scroll, and the stars fall like withered leaves from a vine.

Zephaniah hears God say that he will sweep away everything from the face of the earth, human and beast, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, reversing the order of creation in Genesis. Joel sees the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood. Daniel, the latest of these books, speaks of a time of trouble such as never has been, followed by the awakening of those who sleep in the dust.
versions.caveat: Many of these oracles address judgment on particular nations; reading them as a single end of the world developed in later Jewish and Christian apocalyptic.

versions.title: Seven Suns and the Flood of Dissolution
versions.teaser: Drought, seven blazing suns, fire, then a hundred years of rain.
versions.text:
At the end of a thousand ages, when the earth is exhausted, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa describes the pralaya, the dissolution. A terrible drought lasts a hundred years, and living things perish. Viṣṇu, taking the form of Rudra, drinks up all the waters of the world. The seven rays of the sun become seven suns, and they blaze until the three worlds, the mountains, rivers and oceans, are burned, and the earth is left bare as a tortoise's back. Fire from the breath of the serpent Śeṣa consumes the underworlds.

Then great clouds, the Saṃvartaka, rise up, huge as elephants and roaring, some dark, some the colour of smoke, some yellow, and they pour down rain for a hundred years, until the fire is quenched and the whole universe is one ocean. On those waters Viṣṇu sleeps, on the coils of Śeṣa, until the night of Brahmā ends.

versions.title: The River of Molten Metal
versions.teaser: A falling star, the last battle, and a flood of molten metal.
versions.text:
Zoroastrian tradition divides history into ages, and the last is marked by the coming of the Saoshyant, the final saviour. In the Bundahishn, the evil powers make their last stand. The demons are destroyed one by one, and the meteor Gōchihr falls from the sky onto the earth, which suffers like a sheep attacked by a wolf.

Then fire and the god Airyaman melt the metal in the hills and mountains, and it flows over the earth like a river. Every human being must pass through it. To the righteous it feels like walking through warm milk; to the wicked it is molten metal, and it purges them. Ohrmazd seizes the Evil Spirit, Ahriman, who flees through the hole by which he first broke into creation, and is driven back into the darkness. The serpent Gōchihr burns in the metal, and the stench and filth of hell are burned away.
versions.caveat: The Bundahishn is a Pahlavi compilation of the 9th century CE, though it draws on much older Avestan tradition.

versions.title: Ragnarök
versions.teaser: The wolf swallows Odin, fire takes the world, and earth sinks.
versions.text:
Heimdall blows the Gjallarhorn and the ash Yggdrasil trembles. The wolf Fenrir breaks loose; the world-serpent writhes up onto the land; ships bring the giants and the host of the dead, Loki among them, and Naglfar, made of dead men's nails, breaks loose. From the south comes Surtr with fire, and the bridge Bifröst breaks under his army.

The gods meet their enemies on the plain of Vígríðr. Fenrir swallows Odin, and his son Víðarr avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart. Thor kills the serpent, walks nine steps and falls dead of its venom. Freyr, who gave away his sword, falls to Surtr. Týr and the hound Garmr kill each other, as do Loki and Heimdall. Then, in Völuspá's words: ‘The sun turns black, earth sinks into the sea, the bright stars vanish from heaven; steam rages with fire, and high flame plays against heaven itself.’

versions.title: The End of the Fifth Sun
versions.teaser: Four suns have ended; the fifth will perish in earthquakes.
versions.text:
The Aztecs lived in the fifth age of the world. Four earlier suns had each been destroyed, by jaguars, wind, fiery rain and flood. The present sun is called Nahui Ollin, ‘4 Movement’, and the Legend of the Suns says what will become of it: it will end in earthquakes and famine, and we shall perish.

The danger was felt most at the end of every fifty-two-year cycle. Sahagún's informants describe the New Fire ceremony: all fires are put out, and priests climb the Hill of the Star to drill a new fire on the chest of a sacrificed captive. If the fire failed to kindle, the sun would be destroyed forever, it would be night always, and the tzitzimime, star-demons, would descend to devour humankind. Pregnant women were shut away wearing masks of maguey leaf lest they turn into beasts, and children were kept awake lest they turn into mice.

concepts.summary: An ending is often not the end. After the fire, flood or final battle, many traditions see a new world rising: a green earth lifted from the sea, a renovated creation without death, a new golden age at the turn of the cycle, or a fresh sun lit by divine sacrifice. Cyclical cosmologies, as in India and Mesoamerica, expect renewal as a matter of course; linear ones, as in Iran and Israel, make it a single final perfection. Iranian ideas of resurrection and renovation very probably influenced Jewish and Christian hopes, but the Indic and Mesoamerican cycles are independent traditions.

versions.title: Frashokereti, the Making Wonderful
versions.teaser: The dead rise, drink immortality, and the earth is made level.
versions.text:
The Avestan hymn to the royal glory looks forward to the day when the world will be made ‘wonderful’, frashō: never ageing, never dying, never decaying, ever living and ever thriving, when the dead will rise and immortality come.

The Bundahishn gives the details. The bones of the dead are raised, first those of the first man, Gayōmard, and of the first human couple, and every soul is reunited with its body and recognizes its kin. After the ordeal of molten metal, Ohrmazd and the saviour Saoshyant perform the last sacrifice. From the fat of the bull Hadhayans and the white haoma they prepare the drink of immortality and give it to all people, who become deathless forever. Adults remain forty years old and children fifteen. The metal fills the pit of hell, the mountains are levelled, and the earth becomes a smooth plain where evil can never again enter.
versions.caveat: The detailed scheme is in 9th-century Pahlavi texts; the Avestan hymns give only its outline.

versions.title: New Heavens and a New Earth
versions.teaser: No weeping, long lives, and the wolf grazing with the lamb.
versions.text:
In the last chapters of Isaiah, God announces: ‘I am about to create new heavens and a new earth; the former things shall not be remembered or come to mind.’ Jerusalem will be a joy and its people a delight. No sound of weeping will be heard in it, no infant will live only a few days, and one who dies at a hundred will be thought a youth. People will build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

The animals are made new as well. ‘The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy on all my holy mountain.’ An earlier oracle in the same book gives the picture its most famous form: the wolf dwelling with the lamb, the leopard lying down with the kid, and a little child leading them.
versions.caveat: Isaiah's oracle describes the restoration of Jerusalem in this world; its reading as a new cosmos after the end comes with later apocalyptic, as in Revelation 21.

versions.title: The Savoury Earth
versions.teaser: Radiant beings return to a new world, taste it, and fall.
versions.text:
In the Aggañña Sutta, the Buddha describes what happens when the world, after contracting, expands again. During the contraction most beings are reborn in the realm of Radiance, mind-made, feeding on joy, shining by their own light and moving through the air. When the world re-forms, they return, still radiant. All is water and darkness; there is no sun, no moon, no night or day, no male or female.

Then a savoury earth spreads over the waters, like the skin that forms on boiled milk as it cools, the colour of ghee and sweet as honey. One greedy being tastes it on a finger, and craving arises. As they eat, their radiance fades, and so the sun and moon appear. Their bodies coarsen, differences of beauty and pride arise, the savoury earth disappears, and in time come rice, sex, houses, property and theft. At last the people choose one among them to keep order: the Great Elect, the first king.
versions.caveat: The Buddha tells this partly as a satire on Brahmin claims of divine origin, so its tone is ironic as well as cosmological.

versions.title: Kalki and the Returning Golden Age
versions.teaser: At the end of the Kali age, Viṣṇu comes as Kalki and virtue returns.
versions.text:
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa describes the Kali age, the last and worst of the four, as an age in which wealth alone confers rank, falsehood is the means of success, and kings plunder their subjects. When it is almost over, a portion of Viṣṇu will be born as Kalki, in the house of the Brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas in the village of Śambhala, endowed with eight superhuman powers.

Kalki will destroy the barbarians, thieves and all whose minds are devoted to wickedness, and re-establish righteousness on earth. The minds of those who are alive at the end of the Kali age will become clear as crystal, and they will be the seed of a new humanity who follow the laws of the Kṛta age, the golden age, as the cycle turns again. ‘When the sun, the moon, the lunar asterism Tiṣya and the planet Jupiter are in one mansion,’ the text says, ‘the Kṛta age shall return.’

versions.title: The Green Earth Rises
versions.teaser: The earth rises again from the sea, and golden game-pieces lie in the grass.
versions.text:
In Völuspá the seeress sees the earth rise a second time out of the sea, green again. Waterfalls plunge, and an eagle flies over them hunting fish from the mountainside. The surviving gods meet on the plain of Iðavöllr, where they talk of the world-serpent and remember the great events and the ancient runes of Odin. There, in the grass, they find the wonderful golden game-pieces they had owned in the days of old. Fields bear crops unsown, all ills are healed, and Baldr comes back from the dead, reconciled with his slayer Höðr.

Snorri adds that Víðarr and Váli survive, that Thor's sons Móði and Magni come bearing their father's hammer, and that the sun has borne a daughter before the wolf took her, who now rides her mother's path. Líf and Lífþrasir come out of hiding to repeople the world. Then, in the poem's last lines, a dark dragon flies up, bearing corpses in its feathers.
versions.caveat: Some scholars see Christian influence in Völuspá's renewed world, especially the hall Gimlé and the ‘mighty one’ who comes from above in one manuscript.

versions.title: The Fifth Sun Is Lit
versions.teaser: Bones fetched from the dead, and a pimpled god leaps into the fire.
versions.text:
The fourth sun has ended in a flood, its people turned into fish, and the sky has fallen. The gods raise it up again, and then they must make new people. Quetzalcoatl goes down to Mictlan, the land of the dead, to ask its lord for the precious bones. The lord sets him a trick task, blowing a conch shell with no holes; worms bore holes and bees fly inside to make it sound. Fleeing with the bones, Quetzalcoatl stumbles, and they break. The goddess Cihuacoatl grinds them, Quetzalcoatl bleeds on them, and humans are born.

There is still no sun. At Teotihuacan the gods build a fire, and the humble, pimpled Nanahuatzin leaps into it first; the proud Tecuciztecatl, after hesitating, follows. Nanahuatzin rises as the sun, and Tecuciztecatl as the moon. But the sun will not move until the other gods give their own lives, and only then does the fifth age begin.
